nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
COMMON NAME:  White grunt
Scientific Name: Haemulon plumieri

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthys
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Haemulidae

Other Common Names:  black grunt (312), grunt (312 664), common grunt (867), Key West grunt, ruby red lips (1246), flannelmouth grunt (1248).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Fished commercially throughout its range (1035 1105).  One of the most valuable fish species caught on the Campeche Bank (850).  Usually marketed fresh, and reported by Fischer (791) to be caught primarily in the West Indies especially during the fall and winter.  The species of greatest abundance in the trap fishery of the West Indies (850).

Recreational:  Fished for recreationally throughout the year and throughout its range (850 1035).  Commonly caught on the west coast of Florida, it forms the basic catch of party boats in Monroe, Sarasota, Pinellas, Brevard, Levy, Taylor, and Wakulla counties (850).  Also common in catches on the southeastern Atlantic coast, especially north of Cape Canaveral (850).  Common from South Carolina and south, and reported as a food fish of some importance (312).  Caught primarily by hook and line off the southeastern United States (850), it is also harvested by hand line, seine, and fish traps (791 1219).

Indicator:  None identified

Ecological Role:  Important as energy importers to reef communities because of nocturnal foraging migrations (850).  Because of their abundance, they are probably the major prey of many larger species such as groupers and snappers (850).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Occurs from Chesapeake Bay to Brazil, the Bahamas and the eastern Gulf of Mexico (327 788 850).  Introduced in Bermuda (867).  The most common inshore grunt from the shore to the outer reef in southern Florida and the Bahamas (1112).

Within Study Area:  Throughout Florida waters (791 1219).  Abundant on the west coast of Florida north to Pensacola in the summer (1112).  It is found in the southern IRL near inlets and in adjacent seagrass beds (887 848).


Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Structure associated epibenthic predator found on reefs, near inlets and in inlet associated reefs and grass flats.  Often found singly or in small groups, but school over reefs and gorgonians, particularly during the day (837 848 850 887).

No known migrations other than those primarily associated with foraging (850).  On the west coast of Florida, Moe (947) found that only 2 of 39 tagged fish moved more than 8 km (5 miles), and only 26% moved more than 4.8 km.  In another study, three tagged fish were recovered at the tagging site 4 years later (38).  Reid (581) speculated an early migration of the young into deeper waters.  Little migration has been observed on the patch reefs of the upper Florida Keys (800).  Diurnal-nocturnal foraging migrations have been documented in the Virgin Islands (850).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Eggs and early larvae are pelagic (363).  Juveniles and adults found from the shore to deeper reefs to about 35 m (791), occupying a variety of habitats including reefs inlets grass flats, and mangrove fringes (848 850).

Substrate:  Found on grass flats and the rocky reefs offshore in the Tampa Bay area (664).  Occur over muddy sand bottoms at Cedar Key (581).  On the southeast Atlantic coast found primarily over live bottom shelf areas (850 1084).  Appear to prefer shelf areas with ridges of hard substrate containing soft areas in between (850).  Found on grass beds, sand flats, and reef areas throughout its range (791).  Said to be the most common grunt on shallow turtle grass beds and around red mangroves (363) but not dominant in the IRL area (993).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae:  Eggs reared in the laboratory hatched within 20 hours at 24.2 C (946).

Juvenile/adults:  Considered a warm water species, its geographic distribution is apparently limited by temperature (850).  It is generally absent in shallow water during the winter and early spring (581 789 1029 1034 1246 1248).  Collected in Tampa Bay at temperatures of 22.1 to 23.6 C (664).  In Charlotte Harbor, taken at temperatures of 29.6 to 35 C (789).  Found in the northern Gulf of Mexico in the winter at temperatures as low as 13 C (850), but often found hurt during freezes at Sanibel Island, Florida (836).  Also reported killed by the cold at temperatures of 14 C at Key West (850), and at 11.1 C in Indian River lagoon, Florida (236).

nodes.title: Eggs/Larvae
nodes.body: Juvenile/adults:  Have been recorded from salinities form 18 to 42.8 ppt (1248 363).  Collected in Tampa Bay at salinities from 30.8 to 32.4 ppt (664) and in Charlotte Harbor from 18.6 to 35.7 ppt (789).  In southwest Florida, collected in salinities ranging from 18 to 37 ppt (603).  Juveniles may have a greater tolerance of salinity than adults (850).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Sexual reproduction, gonochoristic, oviparous, pelagic eggs with external fertilization (850).  Apparently sheds eggs in batches over time (850).

Mating/Spawning: Mature during the third year on the Campeche Bank at <18 cm; males mature at a mean size of 20cm FL and females were fully mature at a mean size of 22cm FL (850).  It is reported that on the Florida west coast spawning probably occurs in the spring based on the occurrence of young in the fall (581).  Large numbers of ripe individuals have been reported in the spring, but it appears that all were spent by July (947).  Darcy (850) thought that spawning occurs over much of the year but is concentrated in the spring.  Spawning occurs in April and May on Campeche Bank (850).  Concentrated in the spring at several Caribbean Islands (850).

Fecundity: Unknown.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs/Larvae:  Larvae reared in the laboratory grew at a rate of 0.32 mm/day (946).  Larvae grew from 2.7 mm to 10.0 mm in 20 days and to 12.6 mm in 30 days (946).

Juveniles/Adults:  Juvenile stage begins at 9.5 to 10.0 mm or a little larger (363).  Adults tagged on the Florida west showed a growth rate ranging from 1.4 to 3.6 mm/month (947).  Manooch (1035) presented length-weight equations, and found that females weighed less than males of a similar length.  Von Bertalanffy growth equations are given in Darcy (850).  Maximum adult size is 450 to 460 mm (327 788 874 945).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Very small juveniles pick plankton directly from the water column during the day (1252).  Young fish, as described from a population on the west coast of Florida, feed on copepods and mysids (581).  Carr and Adams (98) found that the young were primarily planktivorous at Crystal River.  Juveniles and adults are nocturnal feeders which eat worms, crustaceans, lamellibranchs, and gastropods (837). Adults described as generalized carnivores which feed mainly on benthic invertebrates (1035), they feed on echinoderms, polychaetes, majid crabs, alpheid shrimp, and isopods (40 1253).  Also feeds on shrimp, crabs and small fish (791 850).

	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Haemulidae

Other Common Names:  black grunt (312), grunt (312 664), common grunt (867), Key West grunt, ruby red lips (1246), flannelmouth grunt (1248).

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Fished commercially throughout its range (1035 1105).  One of the most valuable fish species caught on the Campeche Bank (850).  Usually marketed fresh, and reported by Fischer (791) to be caught primarily in the West Indies especially during the fall and winter.  The species of greatest abundance in the trap fishery of the West Indies (850).

Recreational:  Fished for recreationally throughout the year and throughout its range (850 1035).  Commonly caught on the west coast of Florida, it forms the basic catch of party boats in Monroe, Sarasota, Pinellas, Brevard, Levy, Taylor, and Wakulla counties (850).  Also common in catches on the southeastern Atlantic coast, especially north of Cape Canaveral (850).  Common from South Carolina and south, and reported as a food fish of some importance (312).  Caught primarily by hook and line off the southeastern United States (850), it is also harvested by hand line, seine, and fish traps (791 1219).

Indicator:  None identified

Ecological Role:  Important as energy importers to reef communities because of nocturnal foraging migrations (850).  Because of their abundance, they are probably the major prey of many larger species such as groupers and snappers (850).

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Occurs from Chesapeake Bay to Brazil, the Bahamas and the eastern Gulf of Mexico (327 788 850).  Introduced in Bermuda (867).  The most common inshore grunt from the shore to the outer reef in southern Florida and the Bahamas (1112).

Within Study Area:  Throughout Florida waters (791 1219).  Abundant on the west coast of Florida north to Pensacola in the summer (1112).  It is found in the southern IRL near inlets and in adjacent seagrass beds (887 848).


Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
Structure associated epibenthic predator found on reefs, near inlets and in inlet associated reefs and grass flats.  Often found singly or in small groups, but school over reefs and gorgonians, particularly during the day (837 848 850 887).

No known migrations other than those primarily associated with foraging (850).  On the west coast of Florida, Moe (947) found that only 2 of 39 tagged fish moved more than 8 km (5 miles), and only 26% moved more than 4.8 km.  In another study, three tagged fish were recovered at the tagging site 4 years later (38).  Reid (581) speculated an early migration of the young into deeper waters.  Little migration has been observed on the patch reefs of the upper Florida Keys (800).  Diurnal-nocturnal foraging migrations have been documented in the Virgin Islands (850).

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type: Eggs and early larvae are pelagic (363).  Juveniles and adults found from the shore to deeper reefs to about 35 m (791), occupying a variety of habitats including reefs inlets grass flats, and mangrove fringes (848 850).

Substrate:  Found on grass flats and the rocky reefs offshore in the Tampa Bay area (664).  Occur over muddy sand bottoms at Cedar Key (581).  On the southeast Atlantic coast found primarily over live bottom shelf areas (850 1084).  Appear to prefer shelf areas with ridges of hard substrate containing soft areas in between (850).  Found on grass beds, sand flats, and reef areas throughout its range (791).  Said to be the most common grunt on shallow turtle grass beds and around red mangroves (363) but not dominant in the IRL area (993).

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content:
Eggs/Larvae:  Eggs reared in the laboratory hatched within 20 hours at 24.2 C (946).

Juvenile/adults:  Considered a warm water species, its geographic distribution is apparently limited by temperature (850).  It is generally absent in shallow water during the winter and early spring (581 789 1029 1034 1246 1248).  Collected in Tampa Bay at temperatures of 22.1 to 23.6 C (664).  In Charlotte Harbor, taken at temperatures of 29.6 to 35 C (789).  Found in the northern Gulf of Mexico in the winter at temperatures as low as 13 C (850), but often found hurt during freezes at Sanibel Island, Florida (836).  Also reported killed by the cold at temperatures of 14 C at Key West (850), and at 11.1 C in Indian River lagoon, Florida (236).

sections.heading: Eggs/Larvae
sections.content: Juvenile/adults:  Have been recorded from salinities form 18 to 42.8 ppt (1248 363).  Collected in Tampa Bay at salinities from 30.8 to 32.4 ppt (664) and in Charlotte Harbor from 18.6 to 35.7 ppt (789).  In southwest Florida, collected in salinities ranging from 18 to 37 ppt (603).  Juveniles may have a greater tolerance of salinity than adults (850).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode:  Sexual reproduction, gonochoristic, oviparous, pelagic eggs with external fertilization (850).  Apparently sheds eggs in batches over time (850).

Mating/Spawning: Mature during the third year on the Campeche Bank at <18 cm; males mature at a mean size of 20cm FL and females were fully mature at a mean size of 22cm FL (850).  It is reported that on the Florida west coast spawning probably occurs in the spring based on the occurrence of young in the fall (581).  Large numbers of ripe individuals have been reported in the spring, but it appears that all were spent by July (947).  Darcy (850) thought that spawning occurs over much of the year but is concentrated in the spring.  Spawning occurs in April and May on Campeche Bank (850).  Concentrated in the spring at several Caribbean Islands (850).

Fecundity: Unknown.

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Eggs/Larvae:  Larvae reared in the laboratory grew at a rate of 0.32 mm/day (946).  Larvae grew from 2.7 mm to 10.0 mm in 20 days and to 12.6 mm in 30 days (946).

Juveniles/Adults:  Juvenile stage begins at 9.5 to 10.0 mm or a little larger (363).  Adults tagged on the Florida west showed a growth rate ranging from 1.4 to 3.6 mm/month (947).  Manooch (1035) presented length-weight equations, and found that females weighed less than males of a similar length.  Von Bertalanffy growth equations are given in Darcy (850).  Maximum adult size is 450 to 460 mm (327 788 874 945).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Very small juveniles pick plankton directly from the water column during the day (1252).  Young fish, as described from a population on the west coast of Florida, feed on copepods and mysids (581).  Carr and Adams (98) found that the young were primarily planktivorous at Crystal River.  Juveniles and adults are nocturnal feeders which eat worms, crustaceans, lamellibranchs, and gastropods (837). Adults described as generalized carnivores which feed mainly on benthic invertebrates (1035), they feed on echinoderms, polychaetes, majid crabs, alpheid shrimp, and isopods (40 1253).  Also feeds on shrimp, crabs and small fish (791 850).
